Note: The headings in the text were added by the annotator and are not part of the sutra.

This sutra is excerpted from the chapter on the Ten Virtues and Six Perfections of the Sutra of the Buddha’s Teaching on the Dragon King of the Sea. Spoken in the dragon palace for the dragon king Sagara, it teaches that those who forever abandon the ten evils — killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech, divisive speech, abusive speech, idle speech, greed, anger, and wrong views — and cultivate the ten wholesome deeds gain immeasurable merit and may perfect the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the eighteen unshared qualities, and all the Buddha’s Dharma. As all cities and villages abide upon the great earth and all herbs, plants, and forests grow from it, so this path of the ten wholesome deeds underlies the vehicle of humans, the vehicle of gods, the vehicles of hearers, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas, and all the Buddha’s Dharma, all of which are fulfilled upon this great earth of the ten wholesome deeds. Thus cultivating this path is the most fundamental practice of Buddhism, and both Mahayana and Hinayana regard it as a foundational text.

The Five Vehicles The vehicle of humans, gods, hearers, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas. “Vehicle” means conveyance: the Dharma is like a ferry bearing sentient beings from this shore to the other. The vehicle of humans rides the five precepts and is reborn among humans; the vehicle of gods rides the ten wholesome deeds and is reborn in the heavens; the vehicle of hearers rides the Four Noble Truths and realizes the fruit of an arhat; the vehicle of pratyekabuddhas rides the twelve links of dependent origination and realizes the fruit of a pratyekabuddha; the vehicle of bodhisattvas rides the six perfections and realizes the supreme fruit of buddhahood.

In the sutra the World-Honored One taught: “Dragon King! The bodhisattva has one Dharma that can sever all the suffering of the evil realms. What is it? To dwell day and night in thought, reflection, and observation of wholesome Dharmas, so that they grow from moment to moment and never a trace of the unwholesome mingles in. Then all evils are cut off forever, wholesome Dharmas are perfected, and one always draws near to the Buddhas, bodhisattvas, and the other holy assemblies. Wholesome Dharma means the body of a human, the body of a god, the bodhi of a hearer, the bodhi of a pratyekabuddha, and the unsurpassed bodhi, which all rely on this Dharma as their root and are fulfilled. This Dharma is the path of the ten wholesome karmic actions. What are the ten? To forever abandon killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech, divisive speech, abusive speech, idle speech, greed, anger, and wrong views.”
The Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on the Ten Wholesome Karmic Paths

The Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on the Ten Wholesome Karmic Paths” is the title. “Spoken by the Buddha”: this sutra was spoken by Śākyamuni Buddha. “The ten wholesome karmic actions” are not killing, not stealing, not sexual misconduct, not false speech, not divisive speech, not abusive speech, not idle speech, not greed, not anger, and not wrong views (not ignorance). “Path” (dao) means the way of Dharma, and the sense of a road. “The path of the ten wholesome karmic actions” is the method of cultivating the ten wholesome actions, that is, forever abandoning killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech, divisive speech (stirring up disputes), abusive speech (mocking and harsh words), idle speech (meaningless talk), greed, anger, and wrong views (ignorance). “Sutra” (jing) means the Buddha’s teaching, called sutra in Sanskrit because it threads the meaning of the Dharma so that it is not lost, accords above with the wondrous principle of all Buddhas, and accords below with the capacities of sentient beings.

This sutra chiefly teaches that cultivating the ten wholesome karmic actions is the basic virtue of a student of the Buddha, able to sever the suffering of the three evil realms (animals, hungry ghosts, hells) and being the root for attaining the body of a human, the body of a god, and all the holy fruits (arhat, pratyekabuddha, bodhisattva, buddha).
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Siksnanda of Khotan in the Tang Dynasty
This sutra was translated by the Tripitaka Master Siksnanda, a native of Khotan, in the Tang Dynasty.

Khotan An ancient kingdom of the Western Regions, in western Xinjiang, the region of present-day Hotan. Tripitaka Master A master versed in the three baskets of scripture, discipline, and treatise. Siksnanda A man of Khotan in the Tang Dynasty, versed in both Mahayana and Hinayana and conversant with other schools. In the first year of Zhengsheng (in the year

CE), he brought the Sanskrit Avatamsaka Sutra to Luoyang and, at the command of Empress Wu Zetian, translated it into Chinese with Bodhiruci, Yijing, and others at the Great Universal Emptiness Temple in the eastern capital; this is the new eighty-fascicle Avatamsaka. He also translated the Lankavatara Sutra of the Great Vehicle and the Sutra of Manjusri’s Predictions, nineteen works in 107 fascicles. Eastern Capital In the Tang, Luoyang was the eastern capital; the imperial capital was Chang’an.

blocks.text: I. The Dharma Assembly in the Dragon Palace

inline.s: Thus have I heard. At one time the Buddha was in the palace of the dragon king Sagara, together with eighty thousand great bhiksus and thirty-two thousand bodhisattvas, great beings.
This is what I (Ānanda) heard and saw myself. At that time the Buddha dwelt in the palace of the dragon king Sagara with eight thousand great bhiksus and thirty-two thousand great bodhisattvas.

Thus have I heard This is my (Ānanda’s) own hearing and seeing, a mark of credibility attesting that the sutra was truly spoken by the Buddha and recorded correctly. As the Buddha was about to enter parinirvāṇa he instructed the Venerable Ānanda that when the scriptures were later collected, every sutra should begin with “Thus have I heard”, to show it was spoken by the Buddha and to distinguish it from non-Buddhist scriptures. The “I” is Ānanda, the compiler, the Buddha’s younger cousin born on the night of the Buddha’s enlightenment, who later followed him into homelessness and served as his attendant for twenty-five years, famed as foremost in learning and remembering. After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, when the Venerable Mahakasyapa convened the council in the great stone cave of Magadha, five hundred great arhats gathered and unanimously urged Ānanda to ascend the seat and recite the teaching. Sagara Translated into Chinese as “salt sea”. Great bhiksu A bhiksu of deep resolve and deep practice. Bodhisattva, great being A great bodhisattva, one of deep resolve and deep practice.

blocks.text: II. Thought and Karma Bring About the Realms

inline.s: At that time the World-Honored One said to the dragon king: “All sentient beings, because their thoughts differ, create karma that also differs, and because of this they revolve among the various realms.”

At that time the World-Honored One said to the dragon king: All sentient beings, because their thoughts differ, create karma that differs, and from this comes the wheel of rebirth through the six realms.
At that time That moment (here, when the Buddha began to speak this sutra). World-Honored One An honorific for Śākyamuni Buddha, so called because he is honored by the whole world. Karma (
karma
) in Sanskrit
karman
, and in Pali
kamma

; the sense of doing or making. All our wholesome and unwholesome thoughts, words, and actions are karma. Good thoughts, words, and actions are “wholesome karma”; bad ones are “unwholesome karma”. Karma is also divided into leading karma and completing karma, the “two kinds of karma”. Two kinds of karma Leading karma and completing karma: the karma that draws you to be reborn in a certain realm is leading karma; the karma that determines the quality of that life (wise or foolish, beautiful or ugly, noble or base, long- or short-lived) is completing karma. Various realms “Realm” (qu) means tending or going; as beings receive retribution they always go from cause to fruit, so the six realms are also the six destinies, the places where beings pass by riding on their karma. Revolution among the various realms The wheel of the six destinies, the wheel of the six realms. Six realms Gods, humans, asuras, animals, hungry ghosts, hells; of these gods, humans, and asuras are the three wholesome destinies, and animals, hungry ghosts, and hells the three evil destinies. Asura Translated as “not-god”, having the fortune of a god but not its virtue; fond of war, perpetually at odds with Sakra (lord of the Trayastrimsa heaven), its land having ugly men and beautiful women, its palaces north of Mount Sumeru beneath the sea.

Here the World-Honored One revealed the fundamental cause of rebirth in the six realms — “because their thoughts differ, the karma they create differs” — whereby beings, having different thoughts, create different karma and so receive different retributions, which decides the realm into which a being is reborn and the quality of that life. The Sutra of the Five Sufferings says: “The mind takes hell, the mind takes hungry ghosts, the mind takes animals, the mind takes gods and humans; all that shapes appearance is wrought by the mind.” The Avatamsaka Sutra
Ten Transferences chapter says in verse: “All things in the world, with retributions each different, are all brought about by the power of karma.”
The power of karma The strength of karma: wholesome karma can bring happy results, unwholesome karma painful ones.

Dragon King! Do you see in this assembly, and in the great sea, forms and colors each different from the other? All of this is nothing but the mind creating wholesome and unwholesome bodily, verbal, and mental karma.

Dragon King! Do you see the Buddhas, great bodhisattvas, great arhats, gods, humans, and asuras in this assembly, and the fish, shrimp, turtles, and crabs of every form and color in the great sea — are they not all different from one another? All this difference is none other than the wholesome and unwholesome bodily, verbal, and mental karma brought about by the mind.

This is to say that whether one is reborn in one of the six realms (gods, humans, asuras, animals, hungry ghosts, hells) or in the four holy destinies of arhat, pratyekabuddha, bodhisattva, and buddha, it is all brought about by the mind creating karma. As the “Verse on the Mind” says: “Three dots appear like stars, one hook slants like the moon; wearing fur (the animals) comes forth from it, and becoming a Buddha is also by it.”
Nothing not (mi) Not; without.

And the mind is colorless, cannot be seen or grasped; it is but the gathering of false and vain dharmas, ultimately without a master, without a self or anything belonging to a self. Though each, following its karma, appears differently, yet in reality there is no doer in it. Therefore all dharmas are inconceivable, their nature being like an illusion.

And the mind has no form or color, cannot be seen or grasped; it is only the gathering of false and vain dharmas, ultimately without a real substance (without a master), and does not truly exist (without a self or anything belonging to a self). Though they (the Buddhas, great bodhisattvas, great bhiksus, gods, humans, and asuras of the assembly, and the creatures of every form in the sea), each following their own karma, appear differently, yet in reality there is no true doer. Therefore all dharmas are inconceivable; in their essential nature they are all illusions.

And the mind is colorless, cannot be seen or grasped; it is but the gathering of false and vain dharmas This says the mind is only the gathering of false and vain dharmas and does not truly exist — what the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment calls sentient beings wrongly taking the shadow cast by the six sense-objects upon conditions as their own mind. That sutra says: “All sentient beings, from beginningless time, are in all manner of inversion, like a confused person shifting his position among the four directions; they wrongly take the four great elements as their own body and the shadow cast by the six sense-objects upon conditions as their own mind; like a diseased eye seeing flowers in the sky and a second moon.” Without a self or anything belonging to a self The mind has no self, nor any “belongings of a self” — the mind and the dharmas belonging to it do not truly exist. Here “self” is the mind, and “what belongs to a self” the dharmas possessed by it, i.e. mental phenomena. In Buddhist learning “no-self” means there is no real permanent self. Dharma All things, great or small, formed or formless. Dharmas belonging to the mind Abbreviated as “mental factors” (caitasika), the various mental phenomena possessed by the mind, fifty-one in all. Self-nature like an illusion All dharmas have no substance and are illusions. The Treasury of the Buddha Sutra says: “What is the real character of all dharmas? All dharmas are ultimately empty, nothing existing.” The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sutra says: “All dharmas are like the character of an illusion.” The Diamond Sutra says: “Every characteristic is false and vain.” Real character of all dharmas The actual condition of all dharmas. All dharmas are inconceivable The actual condition of all dharmas can neither be thought by the mind nor spoken in words; in essence it is like the happenings of a dream, false and unreal.

After speaking of phenomenal appearance (“All of this is nothing but the mind creating wholesome and unwholesome bodily, verbal, and mental karma”), the World-Honored One at once spoke of principle (the essential nature of phenomena) — “And the mind is colorless, cannot be seen or grasped; it is but the gathering of false and vain dharmas, ultimately without a master, without a self or anything belonging to a self. Though each, following its karma, appears differently, yet in reality there is no doer in it. Therefore all dharmas are inconceivable, their nature being like an illusion.” Thus both the existent and the non-existent are clearly set forth — phenomenal existence and substantial non-existence both revealed — and phenomena and principle are perfectly fused.

This passage sets forth the essential purport of the Buddha’s teaching — the profound meaning of “phenomena exist while principle is non-existent” and “characteristics exist while substance is non-existent” — explained in detail in the third stage of the “practice as spoken” course, “Prajna dispels delusion”; see the Essential Explanation of the Diamond Sutra, the Essential Explanation of the Heart Sutra, and the Essential Explanation of the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch.

It must be especially noted that, before one clearly understands the dialectical relation of phenomena and principle and of characteristics and substance, and before one can “uphold principle without discarding phenomena and cultivate both together”, one should “prefer to cling to existence than to cling to emptiness”. Do not on any account cling to principle and discard phenomena, for “when phenomena are discarded, principle too is not perfect”, and reckless drifting brings calamity. Remember this! Remember this!

The wise, knowing this, should cultivate wholesome karma; and so the aggregates, realms, and sense-bases into which they are reborn are all upright and comely, so that all who see them are never wearied.

The wise person, knowing that “all of this is nothing but the mind creating wholesome and unwholesome bodily, verbal, and mental karma”, then cultivates wholesome karma; and so the body, mind, and environment into which they are reborn (the aggregates, sense-bases, and realms) are all upright and beautiful, so that all who see them are never wearied.

Should cultivate wholesome karma The “should” is classical usage meaning “following” or “immediately”. Aggregates The five aggregates: form, feeling, perception, conditioning, consciousness; form is the body, the rest the mind. Sense-bases The twelve sense-bases: the six sense organs and the six sense-objects. Realms The eighteen realms: the six sense organs, the six sense-objects, and the six consciousnesses. The six organs: eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, mind. The six objects: form, sound, smell, taste, touch, objects of thought. The six consciousnesses: eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind consciousness — the discernments of seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, feeling, and thinking that arise when the organs meet the objects.

Dragon King! Observe the body of the Buddha, born from hundreds of thousands of millions of merits; his characteristics are adorned, his radiance bright and shining, concealing all the assembly. Even immeasurable millions of independent and Brahma kings would no longer appear. Those who gaze upon the body of the Tathagata — would they not have their eyes dazzled?

Dragon King! Observe the body of the Buddha — born from hundreds of thousands of millions of merits, his characteristics adorned, his radiance bright and shining, so that all the multitudes of the assembly are submerged in his light. Even immeasurable millions of great independent kings and great Brahma kings, though their meritorious radiance be vast, would be submerged in the Buddha’s light, like fireflies beneath the blazing sun, vanishing and unseen. If one gazes upon the body of the Tathagata, how could the eyes not be dazzled and the heart not shaken?

Independent and Brahma kings The great independent heavenly king and the great Brahma heavenly king. The great independent heaven Also called Mahesvara heaven, the highest of the eighteen heavens of the form realm. The great Brahma heaven Brahma means pure; the general name for the form-realm heavens free of sexual desire, whose first-dhyana lord is called the great Brahma heavenly king.

And again observe these great bodhisattvas, their wondrous forms adorned and pure — all born of the cultivation of wholesome karma and merit. And the assemblies of gods, dragons, and the eight classes and others of great power are likewise born of wholesome karma and merit.

Again observe these great bodhisattvas of the assembly — their wondrous forms adorned and pure, all born of their cultivation of wholesome karma and merit. And the assemblies of gods, dragons, and the eight classes and others of great power and authority are likewise born of wholesome karma and merit.

Gods, dragons, and the eight classes Gods and dragons head the eight classes, so the whole is named after them. The eight classes Devas, nagas, yaksas, gandharvas, asuras, garudas, kimnaras, mahoragas. Because human eyes cannot see them, they are also called the “eight classes of unseen beings”; and since gods and dragons are the most excellent, they are also called “gods, dragons, and the eight classes”. Beings of great power Those of great power and authority.

Now all the sentient beings in the great sea, coarse and lowly in form and color, great or small, are all created by the various thoughts of their own minds, doing various unwholesome bodily, verbal, and mental karma; therefore, following their karma, each receives its own retribution.

And all the sentient beings in the great sea, coarse and lowly in form and color, great or small, are all created by the various thoughts of their own minds, doing various unwholesome bodily, verbal, and mental karma; therefore, following their karma, each receives its own retribution.

From this the World-Honored One further clarified the causal principle that thought and karma bring about the realms: the body of the Buddha, bright and shining; the bodies of the bodhisattvas, adorned and pure; and the assemblies of gods, dragons, and the eight classes of great power — all born of wholesome karma and merit; while all the sentient beings of the great sea, coarse and lowly in form, are born of unwholesome karma and base conduct.

You should now always thus cultivate and learn, and also cause sentient beings to understand the law of cause and effect and cultivate wholesome karma. You should, in this, be unwavering in right view, and no longer fall into the views of annihilation or permanence; toward all fields of merit, rejoice in respect and support. Therefore you, too, will obtain the respect and offerings of humans and gods.

From now on, always cultivate and learn in accordance with what I have said, and cause sentient beings to understand the law of cause and effect — that wholesome karma yields wholesome results and unwholesome karma unwholesome results — and to strive in cultivating wholesome karma. Uphold this law of cause and effect throughout your life and work, unshaken by coercion or enticement, and do not fall into the view of annihilation or of permanence. Toward all fields of merit, joyfully respect and make offerings; therefore you, too, will receive the respect and offerings of humans and gods.

The two views of annihilation and permanence The view that body and mind are annihilated at death and never reborn, and the view that they are permanent and never extinguished — both wrong views. Field of merit A field has the sense of growth; one who does good and cultivates virtue is like a farmer tilling and sowing a field, sure to reap a harvest of blessings — hence “field of merit”.

blocks.text: IV. The Path of the Ten Wholesome Karmic Actions

inline.s: Dragon King! You should know that the bodhisattva has one Dharma that can sever all the suffering of the evil realms. What is that one? To dwell day and night in thought, reflection, and observation of wholesome Dharmas, so that they grow and increase from moment to moment, never allowing the slightest residue of the unwholesome to mingle in — this enables all evils to be cut off forever, wholesome Dharmas to be perfected, and one always to draw near to the Buddhas, bodhisattvas, and the other holy assemblies.

Dragon King, you should know: the bodhisattva has one Dharma gate that can sever all the suffering of the evil realms. What is it? In both day and night to be always mindful in reflecting upon and observing wholesome Dharmas, so that they grow and increase moment by moment in one’s own mind and conduct, never allowing the slightest residue of the unwholesome to mingle in — then all evils are cut off forever, wholesome Dharmas are perfected, and one always draws near to the Buddhas, bodhisattvas, arhats, pratyekabuddhas, and the other holy assemblies.

Evil realms Hells, hungry ghosts, animals. Observe Observe the thought, examine the conduct. Reflect upon and observe wholesome Dharmas Reflect upon and observe the phenomena and principle of wholesome Dharmas and examine them in one’s own mind and conduct, with levels of savoring, introspection, earnest practice, and verification; at all times be alert, and with effort summon up the wholesome thought opposite to any unwholesome thought that arises, using the wholesome to subdue the unwholesome — when anger arises summon up loving-kindness and compassion, when envy arises the thought of rejoicing, when indolence arises vigor. Rejoicing To be glad when one sees others doing good, and glad that another is glad. Holy assemblies Arhats, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and Buddhas — the four kinds of attained sages. The Buddhas, bodhisattvas, and the other holy assemblies Here “the other holy assemblies” are those besides the Buddhas and bodhisattvas, namely the arhats and pratyekabuddhas.

What is called wholesome Dharma is that the body of a human, the body of a god, the bodhi of a hearer, the bodhi of a pratyekabuddha, and the unsurpassed bodhi all rely on this Dharma as their root and are fulfilled — therefore it is called wholesome Dharma. This Dharma is the path of the ten wholesome karmic actions. What are the ten? To forever abandon killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech, divisive speech, abusive speech, idle speech, greed, anger, and wrong views.

What is called wholesome Dharma (“wholesome” meaning good and beautiful) is this: to obtain the body of a human, the body of a god, and to realize the fruit of an arhat (the bodhi of a hearer), the fruit of a pratyekabuddha (the bodhi of a pratyekabuddha), and even the fruit of a Buddha (the unsurpassed bodhi), all rely on this Dharma as their root and are fulfilled — therefore it is called wholesome Dharma. This wholesome Dharma is the path of the ten wholesome karmic actions. What is it? To forever abandon killing, stealing, sexual misconduct (adultery), false speech, divisive speech, abusive speech, idle speech, greed, anger, and wrong views (ignorance).

Bodhi Translated as “awakening”, the wisdom that knows the nature of Dharma, the great wisdom of one who has extinguished all afflictions. The three vehicles “Vehicle” means conveyance, a metaphor for the Dharma gate that carries beings across the sea of birth and death to the shore of nirvāṇa. According to dull, middling, and sharp capacities, the Buddha spoke the three teachings of the vehicle of hearers, the vehicle of pratyekabuddhas, and the vehicle of bodhisattvas — respectively the lesser, middle, and great vehicles. Vehicle of hearers One who attains the Way by hearing the Buddha’s voice and teaching is a hearer; taking as its vehicle the Four Noble Truths (suffering, origin, cessation, path) — knowing suffering, cutting off its origin, yearn for cessation, cultivate the path — its highest fruit is the arhat. Vehicle of pratyekabuddhas Also called the vehicle of solitary enlightened ones; contemplating the twelve links of dependent origination and awakening to truth is a pratyekabuddha. First contemplating ignorance through to old age and death, then the cessation of ignorance through to the cessation of old age and death, from the arising and ceasing of these conditions one awakens to neither arising nor ceasing; taking the twelve links as its vehicle, its highest fruit is the pratyekabuddha. Vehicle of bodhisattvas Seeking the unsurpassed bodhi, vowing to save all beings, cultivating the six perfections and the myriad practices; taking the six perfections as its vehicle, its highest fruit is the Buddha. As for forever abandoning Here “capable” means should.

Dragon King! If one abandons killing, one at once attains the ten dharmas of freedom from affliction. What are the ten? One, toward all sentient beings universally bestow fearlessness; two, always give rise to great loving-kindness toward sentient beings; three, cut off forever all the habitual tendencies of anger; four, the body is always free of illness; five, life-span long and far-reaching; six, always guarded by non-humans; seven, always free of evil dreams, joyful in sleep and in waking; eight, extinguish the bonds of enmity and all enmities dissolve of themselves; nine, no fear of the evil realms; ten, at the end of life born in the heavens — these are the ten. If one can dedicate this to anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, then when later one becomes a Buddha, one obtains the Buddha’s lifespan of sovereign freedom.

Dragon King! If one abandons killing, one at once attains the ten dharmas that free one from affliction. What are the ten? First, toward all sentient beings carry out the almsgiving of fearlessness; second, always give rise to great loving-kindness toward sentient beings; third, cut off forever all the habitual tendencies of anger; fourth, the body always free of illness; fifth, life-span long and far-reaching; sixth, always guarded by wholesome spirits; seventh, always free of evil dreams, and whether asleep (sleep) or awake (waking) always joyful; eighth, extinguish the bonds of enmity and all enmities dissolve of themselves; ninth, no fear of falling into the three evil realms; tenth, at the end of life born in the heavens — these are the ten. If one can dedicate this to anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, then when later one becomes a Buddha, one obtains the Buddha’s lifespan of sovereign freedom.

Killing Taking the life of humans, livestock, or any conscious being, the first of the ten evil deeds. The ten dharmas of freedom from affliction The ten dharmas that free one from affliction. Universally bestow fearlessness The almsgiving of fearlessness, using all means to remove others’ dangers and fears; one of the three offerings. The three offerings Offering of wealth, of Dharma, and of fearlessness: the first relieves the poor and suffering with wealth, the second expounds the Buddha’s Dharma one has heard, the third does one’s utmost to remove others’ fear and suffering. Loving-kindness The mind that gives joy to others. Habitual tendencies Bad habits formed over countless eons, become instinctive reactions to circumstances. Non-humans The spirits of the gods, dragons, and eight classes, resembling humans yet not human. Dedication Turning the merit one has cultivated toward some matter or person — to one’s parents, all beings, or the adorning of the Buddha’s Pure Land. Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi The name of the Buddha’s wisdom, translated as “unsurpassed right and perfect enlightenment”, the unsurpassed wisdom that truly and equally knows all truth.
Question: Is eating meat killing?

Answer: Eating meat is killing. For if no one ate meat, naturally no one would slaughter animals to sell. If half the people turned vegetarian, the number of animals slaughtered would surely fall by half. So eating meat participates in killing and is moreover its chief cause; the weight of the karma created may be well imagined.

I and all sentient beings are all within the wheel of rebirth. From beginningless eons we have been mutually giving birth and being raised, and mutually slaughtering one another. They have all been my fathers, mothers, brothers, sisters, or children, and I too have been theirs. They, indeed, by unwholesome karma have become beings of another kind and are slaughtered by me; and I too, by unwholesome karma, have become a being of another kind and have been slaughtered by them. Through long eons, mutually giving birth and mutually slaughtering, with no end. Ordinary people do not know this, but the Tathagata sees it clearly. Now, taught by the Buddha, I myself know these mutual births and slaughters; when I think of it I am overcome with shame and compassion. In the Surangama Sutra the Buddha said: “Sentient beings of the six realms, if their minds do not kill, they do not follow its cycle of birth and death. If you cultivate samādhi intending to escape the dust and toil, and the mind of killing has not been cast out, you cannot emerge from the dust.”
Question: I want to be rid of this evil habit of eating meat, yet I am unable. What should I do?

Answer: On this, Master Yinguang gave an example: “In the tenth year of the Republic I was in Nanjing. Wei Meisun (a member of the Hanlin Academy, then sixty) said to me: ‘Of the Buddha’s Dharma I do believe a part, I am willing to recite the Buddha’s name, and I have read your collected writings; but I simply cannot eat a vegetarian diet.’ I said: ‘The habits of men of wealth and rank are hard to forget. If you wish to eat vegetarian, pray read carefully the essay on the life-releasing pond in my collected writings (A Discourse on the Restoration of the Life-Releasing Pond at Jile Temple, Nanxun); read it again and again, and naturally you will no longer be able to eat meat.’ This was said on the twelfth day of the eighth month. By the tenth month, on his sixtieth birthday, fearing that social ties might be an obstacle, he went to Jinshan (note: Jinshan Temple) to spend his birthday, and upon returning home took up a permanent vegetarian diet at once. The next year he promoted the founding of a Buddha-recitation and life-releasing practice center at Fayun Temple; now he is sixty-six. In charitable works he spares no effort: whether founding an orphanage or giving gruel each year. In the last two years, when war broke out, he gathered the old, weak, women, and children at Fayun Temple, had several dozen awnings built for them, and cooked gruel; when the war ended he gave each travel money according to distance and sent them home — once over a thousand people, another time over two thousand. Each day after the gruel he had them each recite the Buddha’s name and Guanyin.” (From the Collected Writings of Master Yinguang
Reply to the Layman Zhuoren)
The full text and translation of the “A Discourse on the Restoration of the Life-Releasing Pond at Jile Temple, Nanxun” can be found in the appendix.

Further, Dragon King! If one abandons stealing, one at once attains ten dharmas that may be trusted. What are the ten? One, wealth and goods accumulated, which kings, thieves, water, fire, and unloved children cannot scatter and destroy; two, many people love and remember one; three, people do not bully one; four, praised in all ten directions; five, no anxiety about harm; six, a good name spreads abroad; seven, fearless among the multitude; eight, wealth, life, beauty, strength, ease, and happiness, with eloquence complete and lacking nothing; nine, always harboring intent to give; ten, at the end of life born in the heavens — these are the ten. If one can dedicate this to anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, then when later one becomes a Buddha, one realizes the pure great bodhi-wisdom.

Further, Dragon King! If one abandons stealing, then in ten respects one’s fine life is secured. What are the ten? First, wealth and goods accumulated, which officials, bandits, floods, fires, and a prodigal son cannot destroy; second, many people love and remember you; third, no one bullies you; fourth, you are praised in all ten directions; fifth, you need not worry about being harmed; sixth, a good name spreads throughout the four quarters; seventh, you are fearless among the multitude; eighth, you enjoy wealth, longevity, health, capability, and ease, with eloquence complete and lacking nothing; ninth, you always harbor the good intent of giving; tenth, at the end of life you are born in the heavens — these are the ten. If you can dedicate this to anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, then when later you become a Buddha, you realize the pure great bodhi-wisdom.

Stealing In the new translation “taking what is not given”, taking possession of another’s property without permission; one of the ten evil deeds. Further Again, once more, moreover. At once attains ten dharmas that may be trusted Then in ten respects one’s fine life is secured. Kings, thieves, water, fire, and unloved children, cannot scatter and destroy The scriptures often say wealth is held in common by five families — the king, the thief, fire, water, and an evil son — five things that can destroy your wealth: the king (broadly, the powerful) seizes it by force; thieves steal it; floods wash it away; fires burn it; a prodigal son (an unloved child) squanders it. Fearless among the multitude At ease and serene in a crowd. Wealth, life, beauty, strength, ease, and happiness Enjoying wealth, longevity, health, capability, and ease.

Further, Dragon King! If one abandons sexual misconduct, one at once attains four dharmas praised by the wise. What are the four? One, the sense faculties are harmonious and regulated; two, forever free of clamor and agitation; three, praised by the world; four, one’s wife cannot be violated — these are the four. If one can dedicate this to anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, then when later one becomes a Buddha, one obtains the Buddha’s hidden-store mark of a great man.

Further, Dragon King! If one abandons sexual misconduct, one at once attains four dharmas praised by the wise. What are the four? One, a dignified countenance, with body and mind healthy; two, a harmonious and happy family; three, praise from the world; four, one’s wife cannot be violated — these are the four. If one can dedicate this to anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, then when later one becomes a Buddha, one obtains the Buddha’s hidden-store mark of a great man.

[If one abandons wrong conduct] “Wrong conduct” here means sexual misconduct, that is, sexual relations outside marriage. [Attains four dharmas praised by the wise] One obtains four good rewards praised by the wise. [The sense faculties are harmonious and regulated] A dignified countenance, with body and mind healthy. “The sense faculties” are the six faculties: eye, ear, nose, tongue, body and mind; of these, eye, ear, nose, tongue and body refer to the five senses and the physical body, while the mind refers to the mental life. [Forever free of clamor and agitation] A harmonious and happy family. “Clamor” means noise and uproar; “agitation” is auddhatya, a defilement that exalts the mind and leaves it unrestful. [One’s wife cannot be violated] No one can violate one’s wife. [The Buddha’s hidden-store mark of a great man] This is one of the Buddha’s thirty-two marks.

Further, Dragon King! If one abandons false speech, one at once attains eight dharmas praised by the gods. What are the eight? One, the mouth is always pure, with the fragrance of the utpala flower; two, one is trusted and accepted by all the world; three, one’s words become proof, and gods and humans respect and love one; four, one always uses loving words to comfort sentient beings; five, one attains excellent intention and joy, and the three karmas are pure; six, one’s words never err, and the mind is always joyful; seven, one’s words are respected and honored, and gods and humans put them into practice; eight, one’s wisdom is supreme, and none can overcome it — these are the eight. If one can dedicate this to anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, then when later one becomes a Buddha, one at once obtains the Tathāgata’s voice of reality.

Further, Dragon King! If one abandons false speech, one at once attains eight good rewards praised by gods and humans. What are the eight? One, the mouth is always pure, giving forth the fragrance of the utpala flower; two, one is trusted and accepted by all people in the world; three, whatever one says can serve as proof, and gods and humans respect and love one; four, one always comforts sentient beings with gentle and loving words; five, one is most peaceful and joyful, with bodily, verbal and mental karma pure and undefiled; six, one’s words never err, and the mind is always joyful; seven, in speaking one is always respected, and gods and humans put one’s words into practice; eight, one’s wisdom is supreme, and no one can deceive one — these are the eight. If one can dedicate this to anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, then when later one becomes a Buddha, one obtains the Tathāgata’s voice of reality.

[False speech] Speaking what is false and untrue. [Attains eight dharmas praised by the gods] One obtains eight good rewards praised by gods and humans. [The utpala flower] That is, the utpala (blue lotus) flower, which is most fragrant and beautiful. [One’s words become proof] Whatever one says can serve as testimony, because one’s words are always true. [Attains excellent intention and joy, and the three karmas are pure] One is most peaceful and joyful, with bodily, verbal and mental karma pure and undefiled.

Further, Dragon King! If one abandons divisive speech, one at once attains five indestructible dharmas. What are the five? One, one attains an indestructible body, because none can harm it; two, one attains indestructible followers, because none can divide them; three, one attains indestructible trust, because one accords with one’s own karma; four, one attains indestructible Dharma practice, because what one cultivates is firm; five, one attains an indestructible good teacher, because one does not deceive or delude — these are the five. If one can dedicate this to anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, then when later one becomes a Buddha, one obtains a true retinue, and all demons and non-Buddhists cannot destroy it.

Further, Dragon King! If one abandons divisive speech — no longer carrying tales to set others at variance — one at once attains five good rewards that none can injure or destroy. What are the five? One, one attains an indestructible body, because no one can harm one; two, one’s relations with one’s followers are harmonious, because no one can divide them; three, one’s good repute never suffers harm, because one has not created the karma of divisive speech, and others will not use divisive speech to harm one either; four, one’s own practice is not destroyed, because one is pure and single-minded, never setting others at variance, so that one’s practice is firm and immovable; five, no one will destroy the bond between one and one’s good teachers, because one has not set others at variance or deluded them, and so one does not meet with such retribution — these are the five. If one can dedicate this wholesome karma to anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, then when later one becomes a Buddha, one’s attendant disciples all cultivate the true Dharma, and all demons and non-Buddhists cannot destroy it.

[Divisive speech] Carrying tales to set others at variance. [Because one accords with one’s own karma] What one does to others (not speaking divisively) will in the end return to oneself (others will not speak divisively of one either). “One’s own karma” here means not speaking divisively.

Further, Dragon King! If one abandons harsh speech, one at once accomplishes eight kinds of pure karma. What are the eight? One, one’s words are never untimely or unfit; two, all one’s words are beneficial; three, one’s words always accord with principle; four, one’s words are wonderful; five, one’s words are accepted with delight; six, one’s words are trusted; seven, one’s words are beyond reproach; eight, one’s words are wholly loving and joyful — these are the eight. If one can dedicate this to anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, then when later one becomes a Buddha, one is complete in the Tathāgata’s mark of the Brahma voice.

Further, Dragon King! If one abandons harsh speech, one at once accomplishes eight kinds of pure and wholesome karma. What are the eight? One, one’s words are never untimely or unfit; two, all one says benefits sentient beings; three, all one says accords with principle; four, one’s words are wonderful; five, whatever one says others gladly accept; six, one’s words command trust; seven, one’s speech is dignified, beyond censure or mockery; eight, one’s words are wholly filled with love and joy — these are the eight. If one can dedicate this wholesome karma to anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, then when later one becomes a Buddha, one is complete in the Tathāgata’s mark of the Brahma voice: the voice is harmonious and elegant, reaching both near and far, heard everywhere.

[Harsh speech] Reviling and mocking others with poisonous words. [Pure karma] Pure and wholesome karma. [Untimely or unfit] Untimely and unfit. [One’s words are accepted with delight] What one says can make others gladly accept it. [One’s words are trusted] What one says can inspire trust. [The mark of the Brahma voice] The mark of the Brahma voice, profound and far-reaching, among the Buddha’s thirty-two marks: the voice is harmonious and elegant, reaching both near and far, heard everywhere.

Further, Dragon King! If one abandons idle talk, one at once accomplishes three certainties. What are the three? One, one is certainly loved by the wise; two, one can certainly answer questions truthfully with wisdom; three, one is certainly supreme in dignity and virtue among gods and humans, without any falsehood — these are the three. If one can dedicate this to anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, then when later one becomes a Buddha, all the predictions the Tathāgata has bestowed will not have been in vain.

Further, Dragon King! If one abandons idle talk, one at once accomplishes three certain benefits. What are the three? One, one is certainly loved by the wise; two, one can certainly answer questions truthfully with wisdom; three, one is certainly supreme in dignity and virtue among gods and humans, without any falsehood — these are the three. If one can dedicate this wholesome karma to anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, then when later one becomes a Buddha, all the predictions one has received from the Tathāgata will not be cast away in vain.

[Idle talk] Tainted and defiled speech, meaningless speech, and words containing lewd intent. [Three certainties] Three certain benefits. [Prediction] The Buddha’s fore-recording of the name of a sentient being who has aroused the great mind: after so many ages, in such and such a place and land, one will become such and such a Buddha. [In vain] Cast away to no purpose.

Further, Dragon King! If one abandons covetousness, one at once accomplishes five kinds of mastery. What are the five? One, mastery of the three karmas, because the sense faculties are complete; two, mastery of wealth, because no enemy or thief can seize it; three, mastery of merit, because whatever the mind desires is at hand; four, mastery of royal position, because rare and wondrous things are all offered to one; five, whatever one obtains surpasses what one originally sought, a hundred times more excellent, because in the past one was neither stingy nor envious — these are the five. If one can dedicate this to anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, then when later one becomes a Buddha, one is uniquely honored in the three realms, and all revere and support one.

Further, Dragon King! If one abandons covetousness, one at once accomplishes five kinds of mastery. What are the five? One, mastery of the three karmas (bodily, verbal and mental karma), because the moral discipline of the six faculties is complete; two, mastery of wealth, because no enemy or thief can seize it; three, mastery of merit, because whatever the mind desires, all things are at hand; four, mastery of royal position, because rare and wondrous things are all offered to one; five, whatever one obtains far surpasses what one originally sought, a hundred times over, because in the past one was neither stingy nor envious — these are the five. If one can dedicate this wholesome karma to anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, then when later one becomes a Buddha, one is uniquely honored in the three realms, and all revere and support one.

[Mastery] Penetrating without obstruction. [The sense faculties are complete] The moral discipline of the six faculties is complete: the eye does not crave visual objects, the ear does not crave sounds, the nose does not crave fragrances, the tongue does not crave flavors, the body does not crave tangibles, and the mind does not crave mental objects. [Surpasses what one originally sought] Exceeds what one originally sought.

The Lotus Sutra says: “The cause of all suffering is covetousness.” Covetousness is the source of ten thousand evils: at the least it ruins a person, at the most it ruins a nation. Greed for wealth, greed for beauty, greed for power, greed for fame — greed upon greed, beyond reckoning — has made us follow our desires and chase after objects, and so we have sunk to where we are today. Now, to escape the sea of suffering and return to the source, we must put forth great effort in departing from covetousness; as the saying goes, to catch a bandit one must first catch their leader. To seek anything is suffering; only when there is nothing sought does suffering gradually subside. When human desire is extinguished, the mind of the Way arises. The Sutra of Forty-Two Chapters Spoken by the Buddha says: “When the World-Honored One had accomplished the Way, he thought thus: freedom from desire and stillness is the most supreme.” The Laṅkāvatāra Sutra says: “The Sage’s contemplation of stillness — this is to be free from birth; this is called non-appropriation, pure in this life and the next.”

Further, Dragon King! If one abandons anger, one at once attains eight dharmas of joyful mind. What are the eight? One, a mind free of the wish to injure or afflict; two, a mind free of anger; three, a mind free of contention and litigation; four, a mind gentle, straightforward and true; five, one attains the loving mind of the noble ones; six, one always acts for the benefit of others and brings peace to their minds; seven, one’s bodily form is dignified and all revere one; eight, because one is harmonious and patient, one is swiftly born in the Brahma world — these are the eight. If one can dedicate this to anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, then when later one becomes a Buddha, one attains the Buddha’s unobstructed mind, and those who behold one never tire of it.

Further, Dragon King! If one abandons anger, one at once attains eight dharmas of joyful mind. What are the eight? One, no mind to injure or anger others; two, a mind free of anger; three, a mind free of contention and litigation; four, a mind gentle, straightforward and true; five, one attains the loving mind of the noble ones; six, one always acts for the benefit of sentient beings and comforts and settles their minds; seven, one’s bodily form is dignified and all revere one together; eight, because one is harmonious and patient, one is swiftly born in the Great Brahma heaven — these are the eight. If one can dedicate this to anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, then when later one becomes a Buddha, one attains the Buddha’s unobstructed mind, and those who behold one never tire of it.

[Anger] Toward circumstances that go against one’s feelings and do not accord with one’s wishes, the mind gives rise to fury. Anger is a great taboo for a practitioner; hence it is said, “When a single thought of anger arises, ten thousand gates of obstruction open” and “anger burns down the forest of merit.” [Contention and litigation] Disputing and arguing. [A mind gentle, straightforward and true] A mind gentle, plain and upright. [The Brahma world] The Great Brahma heaven.

Further, Dragon King! If one abandons wrong views, one at once accomplishes ten dharmas of merit. What are the ten? One, one attains true and good intention and joy, and true and good companions; two, one deeply believes in cause and effect, and would rather lose life and body than do evil; three, one takes refuge only in the Buddha, not in gods and the like; four, with a straightforward mind and right view, one forever leaves the net of doubt about good and ill fortune; five, one is always born among humans or gods, and never again falls into evil realms; six, one’s measureless merit and wisdom increase and excel more and more; seven, one forever leaves the wrong path and walks the noble path; eight, one does not give rise to the view of a self, and abandons all evil karma; nine, one dwells in unobstructed view; ten, one does not fall into the difficulties — these are the ten. If one can dedicate this to anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, then when later one becomes a Buddha, one swiftly realizes all Buddha-Dharmas and accomplishes sovereign spiritual powers.

Further, Dragon King! If one abandons wrong views, one at once accomplishes ten dharmas of merit. What are the ten? One, one obtains true good teachers to serve as masters, and companions of loving heart and honest, generous character; two, one deeply believes in cause and effect, and would rather sacrifice one’s own life than do evil; three, one takes refuge only in the Buddha, and not in gods and spirits other than the Buddha; four, one has a straightforward mind untouched by gain or loss and right views that accord with truth, and so one never lives in fear, doubting fortune and doubting calamity; five, one is always born in the human or heavenly path, and never again falls into evil realms; six, one’s measureless merit and wisdom increase and excel more and more; seven, one forever leaves the wrong path and walks the noble path; eight, one does not give rise to the wrong view that holds the body to be real (one does not give rise to the view of a self), and one stays far from all evil karma; nine, one’s views are always penetrating and unobstructed (one dwells in unobstructed view); ten, one does not suffer the eight difficulties — these are the ten. If one can dedicate this to anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, then when later one becomes a Buddha, one swiftly realizes all Buddha-Dharmas and accomplishes sovereign spiritual powers.

[Wrong view] This is delusion: the mind and nature are benighted, without the wisdom that comprehends matters and their principles, and one’s thoughts and views run counter to the truth. [One attains true and good intention and joy] One attains true joy wholly filled with a compassionate heart. [One attains true and good companions] One obtains true good teachers to serve as masters, and companions of loving heart and honest, generous character. [One deeply believes in cause and effect, and would rather lose life and body than do evil] One deeply believes in cause and effect, and would rather sacrifice one’s own life than do evil. For life lasts only this one span, whereas the retribution of evil karma is fruit drawing forth further causes and causes attracting further fruits, life after life, requital answering requital, without end.

[One does not fall into the difficulties] One does not suffer the eight difficulties. [The eight difficulties] The eight places and circumstances in which it is difficult to see and hear the Buddha-Dharma, namely: the hells, the hungry ghosts, the animals, the continent of Uttarakuru, the heaven of no thought, being blind, deaf, or dumb, worldly wisdom and clever argument, and before or after a Buddha. Among these, the hells, hungry ghosts and animals belong to the three evil realms; because their karmic obstruction is too heavy, it is very hard for them to see and hear the Buddha-Dharma. The people of Uttarakuru have great blessings, but they do not understand the Buddha-Dharma, and so cannot end birth and death. The heaven of no thought is a place where non-Buddhists are born; the people there likewise cannot end birth and death. Those afflicted with blindness, deafness or dumbness naturally cannot see or hear the Buddha-Dharma. As for worldly wisdom and clever argument, this is when worldly people rely on petty cleverness, refuse to humble themselves and practice, and may even slander the Buddha-Dharma. Those born before the period when the Buddha-Dharma dwells in the world, or after it, likewise cannot hear the Buddha-Dharma. (The period during which Śākyamuni Buddha’s Dharma dwells in the world is twelve thousand years: the True Dharma period of one thousand years, the Semblance Dharma period of one thousand years, and the Dharma-Ending period of ten thousand years.)
In this section the World-Honored One reveals the great benefits obtained by cultivating the three wholesome karmas of body, speech and mind.

blocks.text: 1. Cultivating the Wholesome Karma of the Body

inline.s: [Then the World-Honored One again addressed the Dragon King: If a bodhisattva, relying on this wholesome karma, in the time of cultivating the Way, is able to abandon killing and practice giving, he will always be rich in wealth and treasures, and none can seize them; he will be long-lived and not die young, and will not be harmed by any enemy or thief.]
This speaks of the great benefits obtained by abandoning killing (not taking life).

[Abandoning taking what is not given, and practicing giving, he will always be rich in wealth and treasures, and none can seize them; he will be supreme and without equal, and will be able to gather and perfect the treasury of all Buddha-Dharmas.]
This speaks of the great benefits obtained by abandoning taking what is not given (not stealing).
[Treasury of Dharma] The teaching spoken by the Buddha.

[Abandoning the unchaste life, and practicing giving, he will always be rich in wealth and treasures, and none can seize them; his household will be chaste and harmonious, and no one will be able to look upon his mother and wife with desire.]
This speaks of the great benefits obtained by abandoning the unchaste life (not committing sexual misconduct).

[His household will be chaste and harmonious, and no one will be able to look upon his mother and wife with desire] His household is chaste and harmonious, and no one can look upon his mother and wife with a mind of sexual desire.

blocks.text: 2. Cultivating the Wholesome Karma of Speech

inline.s: [Abandoning false and deceptive speech, and practicing giving, he will always be rich in wealth and treasures, and none can seize them; he will be free of all slander, will gather and uphold the true Dharma, and whatever he vows will surely be fulfilled.]
This speaks of the great benefits obtained by abandoning false and deceptive speech (not lying).

[Abandoning divisive speech, and practicing giving, he will always be rich in wealth and treasures, and none can seize them; his followers will be harmonious, of one mind and one joy, and there will never be discord or contention.]
This speaks of the great benefits obtained by abandoning divisive speech (not speaking in two tongues).
[Never any discord or contention] No awkwardness or quarreling at all.

[Abandoning coarse and harsh speech, and practicing giving, he will always be rich in wealth and treasures, and none can seize them; in every assembly all joyfully take refuge in him, believe and accept all his words, and none oppose or reject them.]
This speaks of the great benefits obtained by abandoning coarse and harsh speech (not speaking harshly).

[Abandoning meaningless speech, and practicing giving, he will always be rich in wealth and treasures, and none can seize them; his words will not be spoken in vain, all will respectfully accept them, and he will be able, by skillful means, to sever all doubts.]
This speaks of the great benefits obtained by abandoning meaningless speech (not speaking idly).
[He will be able, by skillful means, to sever all doubts] He can sever all doubts with skillful means.

blocks.text: 3. Cultivating the Wholesome Karma of Mind

inline.s: [Abandoning a covetous mind, and practicing giving, he will always be rich in wealth and treasures, and none can seize them; he will give away and relinquish all that he has, his faith and understanding will be firm, and he will possess great power.]
This speaks of the great benefits obtained by abandoning a covetous mind (not being greedy).

[Abandoning a wrathful mind, and practicing giving, he will always be rich in wealth and treasures, and none can seize them; he will swiftly accomplish for himself the unobstructed wisdom of mind, and his sense faculties will be noble and fair, so that all who see him respect and love him.]
This speaks of the great benefits obtained by abandoning a wrathful mind (not being angry).
[His sense faculties will be noble and fair] His bodily form is dignified and his mind is beautiful.

[Abandoning a perverse and inverted mind, and practicing giving, he will always be rich in wealth and treasures, and none can seize them; he will always be born into families of right view, reverence and faith, he will see the Buddha, hear the Dharma, and make offerings to the Saṅgha, and he will never forget or lose the great bodhi mind.]
This speaks of the great benefits obtained by abandoning a perverse and inverted mind (not being deluded).
[Thus it is that when the great being cultivates the bodhisattva path, practicing the ten wholesome karmas and adorning them with giving, the great benefits he obtains are like this.]

This is to say that when the great being (a general term for the bodhisattva) cultivates the bodhisattva path, practicing the ten wholesome karmas to adorn himself, the great benefits he obtains are as many as this.

This short passage serves as a link between what precedes and what follows: it sums up the various great benefits obtained by cultivating the ten wholesome karmas above, and opens the way to the various adornments accomplished by cultivating the ten wholesome karmas below.

[The bodhisattva path] The path cultivated by the bodhisattva, that is, the path of benefiting oneself and benefiting others. [Adorning them with giving] To adorn oneself. “Giving” means practicing; “adornment” means embellishing, perfecting, accomplishing.

blocks.text: VI. The Adornment of the Ten Wholesome Karmas

inline.s: Below, the World-Honored One reveals that the ten wholesome karmas can serve as every kind of adornment.

[Dragon King! To speak in brief: practicing the path of the ten wholesome karmas, when adorned by precepts, can produce all the meaning and benefit of Buddha-Dharmas and fulfill the great vows; when adorned by patience, one attains the Buddha’s perfect voice and is complete in all marks; when adorned by diligence, one can destroy the hosts of demons and enter the treasury of Buddha-Dharmas; when adorned by concentration, one can give rise to mindfulness and wisdom, shame, and tranquillity; when adorned by wisdom, one can sever all discriminating and false views.]
This speaks of how cultivating the ten wholesome karmas brings adornment by the six perfections, and thereby many kinds of great benefit.

[The six perfections] The six practices by which one may cross from this shore of the suffering of birth and death to the other shore of the bliss of nirvāṇa: giving, precepts, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and prajñā. Giving can cross over stinginess and greed; precepts can cross over transgression; patience can cross over anger; diligence can cross over indolence; meditative concentration can cross over distraction; prajñā can cross over delusion.

blocks.text: 2. Adornment by the Four Immeasurable Minds

inline.s: [Adorned by loving-kindness, one does not give rise to the wish to harm any sentient being. Adorned by compassion, one pities all sentient beings and never tires of or abandons them. Adorned by joy, one sees those who cultivate goodness without any resentment or envy. Adorned by equanimity, toward circumstances both favorable and adverse one has no mind of love or hate.]
Cultivating the ten wholesome karmas brings adornment by the four immeasurable minds (loving-kindness, compassion, joy and equanimity).

[The four immeasurable minds] The immeasurable mind of loving-kindness, the immeasurable mind of compassion, the immeasurable mind of joy, and the immeasurable mind of equanimity. To give all sentient beings happiness is called the “immeasurable mind of loving-kindness”; to pull all sentient beings out of suffering is called the “immeasurable mind of compassion”; to see others do good or escape suffering and attain happiness, and to feel deep joy, is called the “immeasurable mind of joy”; and to relinquish the three minds above without clinging to them, or else to be equal toward enemy and kin, giving rise to neither love nor hate, is called the “immeasurable mind of equanimity.”

blocks.text: 3. Adornment by the Four Means of Gathering

inline.s: [Adorned by the four means of gathering, one always diligently gathers and transforms all sentient beings.]

Cultivating the ten wholesome karmas brings adornment by the four means of gathering (giving, loving words, beneficial conduct, and working together), so that one always diligently gathers and transforms all sentient beings.

[The four means of gathering] Giving, loving words, beneficial conduct, and working together. The means of giving is this: toward those who set great store by wealth, one practices the giving of goods; toward those who set great store by knowledge, one practices the giving of Dharma — so that the affection between the two deepens by degrees, and one attains the goal of transforming the other. The means of loving words is this: according to the capacities of sentient beings, one speaks to them with gentle and loving words, so that they give rise to joy, feel one to be amiable and approachable, and draw near to one, so that one attains the goal of transforming them. The means of beneficial conduct is this: one who cultivates the bodhisattva path must make all actions of body, speech and mind beneficial to others, and by conduct that harms oneself to benefit others, transform sentient beings so that they cultivate the Buddha-way together, so that one attains the goal of saving others. The means of working together is this: one who cultivates the bodhisattva path must go deep among every level of society, come into contact with people of every trade and profession, become their friend, work alongside them, and, when the time and conditions are fitting, transform them. In saving and ferrying sentient beings across, a bodhisattva must first practice these four means of gathering, so that beings love, respect and trust one; only then can they listen to one’s guidance and cultivate the Buddha-way.

blocks.text: 4. Adornment by the Thirty-Seven Factors of Enlightenment

inline.s: In this section the World-Honored One reveals that cultivating the ten wholesome karmas brings adornment by the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment. The “thirty-seven factors of enlightenment” are: the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of spiritual power (the bases of miraculous power), the five roots, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path. The Vimalakīrti Sutra
Buddha Land Chapter says: “The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are the bodhisattva’s Pure Land.”
[Adorned by the foundations of mindfulness, one is well able to cultivate the contemplation of the four foundations of mindfulness.]
Adorned by the four foundations of mindfulness, one is well able to cultivate the contemplation of the four foundations of mindfulness.

[The four foundations of mindfulness] Also called the four abidings of mindfulness: the foundation of mindfulness of the body, of feeling, of mind, and of dharmas. The foundation of mindfulness of the body is the contemplation that the body is impure; the foundation of mindfulness of feeling is the contemplation that feeling is suffering; the foundation of mindfulness of mind is the contemplation that mind is impermanent; the foundation of mindfulness of dharmas is the contemplation that dharmas are without self. All four contemplations take wisdom as their substance; by the power of wise contemplation they settle the mind upon the path-Dharmas, making it right and not perverse.
[Adorned by right effort, one can wholly sever all unwholesome dharmas and accomplish all wholesome dharmas.]
Adorned by the four right efforts, one can wholly sever all unwholesome dharmas and accomplish all wholesome dharmas.

[The four right efforts] To cause evil already arisen to be cut off; to cause evil not yet arisen not to arise; to cause good not yet arisen to arise; to cause good already arisen to increase. One applies diligence and effort to these four path-Dharmas, so as to spur on body, speech and mind to cut off evil and give rise to good.
[Adorned by the bases of spiritual power, one always makes body and mind tranquil, at ease and happy.]
Adorned by the four bases of spiritual power, one always makes body and mind tranquil, at ease and happy.

[The four bases of spiritual power] Also called the four bases of miraculous power; originally four kinds of meditative concentration, by the cultivation of which one can at will develop spiritual powers. One, the base of spiritual power of desire: the desire to cultivate the Way and reach the fruit increases. Two, the base of spiritual power of mindfulness: mindfulness after mindfulness is single-minded and dwells in right principle. Three, the base of spiritual power of effort: one advances diligently and directly, with no interruption of one’s work. Four, the base of spiritual power of wisdom: true illumination free of delusion, with the mind undistracted.
[Adorned by the five roots, one’s deep faith is firm, one is diligent and never indolent, one is always free of delusion, one is still and well-regulated, and one severs all defilements.]
Adorned by the five roots, one’s deep faith is firm, one is diligent and never indolent, one is always free of delusion, one is still and well-regulated, and one severs all defilements.

[The five roots] The root of faith, the root of effort, the root of mindfulness, the root of concentration, and the root of wisdom. Because faith, effort, mindfulness, concentration and wisdom are the roots from which the noble path is born, they are called the “five roots.”
[Adorned by the powers, all enmity is wholly destroyed, and none can destroy one.]
Adorned by the five powers, all enmity is wholly destroyed, and none can destroy one.

[The five powers] The strength that arises when the five roots (the roots of faith, effort, mindfulness, concentration and wisdom) are firm is called the “five powers”: the power of faith, the power of diligence, the power of mindfulness, the power of concentration, and the power of wisdom. The power of faith is the growth of the root of faith, which can destroy all wrong beliefs; the power of diligence is the growth of the root of diligence, which can destroy bodily indolence; the power of mindfulness is the growth of the root of mindfulness, which can destroy all wrong thoughts; the power of concentration is the growth of the root of concentration, which can destroy all scattered thinking; the power of wisdom is the growth of the root of wisdom, which can destroy all delusions of the three realms.
[Adorned by the factors of enlightenment, one is always good at awakening to all dharmas.]
Adorned by the seven factors of enlightenment, one is always good at awakening to all dharmas.

[The seven factors of enlightenment] Also called the seven limbs of bodhi; they are the seven kinds of awakening manifested from the five roots and five powers. One, the limb of bodhi of discerning dharmas: with wisdom one discerns the true from the false in dharmas. Two, the limb of bodhi of diligence: with a courageous mind one wholeheartedly puts the true Dharma into practice. Three, the limb of bodhi of joy: the mind attains the wholesome Dharma and gives rise to joy. Four, the limb of bodhi of tranquillity: ridding body and mind of coarse and heavy defilements, one attains ease and happiness. Five, the limb of bodhi of mindfulness: at every moment one keeps the true Dharma in mind, so that concentration and wisdom are equal. Six, the limb of bodhi of concentration: the mind rests on a single object without distraction. Seven, the limb of bodhi of equanimity: relinquishing all false and delusive dharmas, one wholeheartedly puts the true Dharma into practice.
[Adorned by the right path, right wisdom is always present before one.]
Adorned by the eightfold noble path, right wisdom is always present before one.

[The eightfold noble path] The eight path-Dharmas of the noble ones. One, right view, that is, correct knowledge and understanding. Two, right thought, that is, correct thinking. Three, right speech, that is, proper words. Four, right action, that is, proper conduct. Five, right livelihood, that is, a proper profession or way of life. Six, right effort, that is, correct endeavor. Seven, right mindfulness, that is, correct recollection. Eight, right concentration, that is, correct meditative concentration. By cultivating this eightfold noble path one can realize the fruit of arhatship.

blocks.text: 5. Adornment by Calm Abiding, Insight and Skillful Means

inline.s: This section speaks of how cultivating the ten wholesome karmas brings adornment by calm abiding, adornment by insight, and adornment by skillful means.
[Adorned by calm abiding, one can wholly wash away all fetters and afflictions.]
Adorned by calm abiding, one can wholly wash away all defilements.

[Calm abiding] In Sanskrit, śamatha: the mind is settled and stilled upon one point. [Fetters and afflictions] Fetters and afflictions. Both “fetter” and “affliction” are other names for defilement: defilement can bind body and mind and form the bitter fruit, and so is called a “fetter”; it can cause sentient beings to sink into the sea of suffering of birth and death, and so is also called an “affliction.”
[Adorned by insight, one can know things as they are, the self-nature of all dharmas.]
Adorned by insight, one can know things as they are, the self-nature of all dharmas.
[Insight] In Sanskrit, vipaśyanā: to observe matters and their principles with right wisdom.
[Adorned by skillful means, one swiftly attains fulfillment, the bliss of the conditioned and the unconditioned.]
Adorned by skillful means, one swiftly attains the perfect accomplishment of the bliss of the conditioned and the unconditioned.
[Skillful means] The devices, methods or words adopted in order to guide and teach sentient beings.

[Dragon King, you should know: this tenfold wholesome karma can even cause the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the eighteen unique dharmas, and all Buddha-Dharmas to be wholly perfected. Therefore you should diligently cultivate and learn.]

After enumerating the various adornments that the ten wholesome karmas can accomplish, the World-Honored One here further says: this tenfold wholesome karma can even cause the Buddha’s ten powers, four fearlessnesses, eighteen unique dharmas, and all Buddha-Dharmas to be wholly perfected. He then admonishes the assembly: therefore you should diligently cultivate and learn.

[The ten powers] The ten kinds of power possessed by the Tathāgata. One, the power of knowing what is possible and impossible: the power of knowing the principle and the non-principle of all things. Two, the power of knowing the karmic retributions of the three times: the power of knowing the causal retributions of the three times of all sentient beings. Three, the power of knowing all meditative states, liberations and samādhis: the power of knowing the various meditative concentrations, liberations and samādhis. Four, the power of knowing the superiority and inferiority of the faculties: the power of knowing the superiority or inferiority of sentient beings’ faculties and the greatness or smallness of the fruits they attain. Five, the power of knowing the various understandings: the power of universally knowing the different understandings of sentient beings. Six, the power of knowing the various realms: the power of universally knowing the different realms of sentient beings. Seven, the power of knowing all the paths leading to the goal: the power of knowing the causes and effects of the paths walked by all sentient beings. Eight, the power of the unobstructed divine eye: the power of seeing with the divine eye the birth and death of sentient beings and the conditions of their good and evil karma, without obstruction. Nine, the power of knowing past lives and the undefiled: the power of knowing sentient beings’ past lives and of knowing the undefiled nirvāṇa. Ten, the power of knowing the forever-ended habitual tendencies: the power of knowing things as they are, that the residual traces of all false delusion are forever cut off and never arise again.

[The Four Fearlessnesses] Fearlessness is a mind that knows no dread in teaching others. The Buddha has four fearlessnesses. First, fearlessness as to omniscience: in the midst of the assembly the Buddha openly declares himself to be the all-knowing one, with a mind free of fear. Second, fearlessness as to the extinction of the outflows: in the midst of the assembly the Buddha openly declares that he has utterly extinguished all defilements, with a mind free of fear. Third, fearlessness as to speaking of what obstructs the path: in the midst of the assembly the Buddha openly declares the various obstructive dharmas — delusion, karma, and the like — with a mind free of fear. Fourth, fearlessness as to speaking of the path that ends suffering: in the midst of the assembly the Buddha openly declares the true paths that end all suffering — precepts, concentration, wisdom, and so forth — with a mind free of fear.

[The Eighteen Unique Dharmas] These are the eighteen dharmas of merit that belong to the Buddha alone; because they are confined to the Buddha and are not shared by the three vehicles, they are called the “unique dharmas.” First, no error of body: since countless kalpas the Buddha has always cultivated his body through precepts, concentration, wisdom and compassion; because his merit is complete and all defilements are exhausted, this is called “no error of body.” Second, no error of speech: the Buddha possesses measureless wisdom and eloquence, and every word that issues from the Buddha’s golden mouth accords, character by character, with truth; this is called “no error of speech.” Third, no error of mindfulness: the Buddha possesses the supreme, profound and wondrous concentration; his mind is not scattered but abides constantly in samādhi, dwelling nowhere with regard to all dharmas; therefore this is called “no error of mindfulness.” Fourth, no differing thought: toward sentient beings the Buddha saves universally and equally, with a mind free of discrimination; this is called “no differing thought.” Fifth, no unsettled mind: whether walking, standing, sitting or lying down, the Buddha never departs from profound samādhi; this is called “no unsettled mind.” Sixth, no knowing-and-yet-abandoning: the Buddha teaches and saves sentient beings, saying whatever he knows with nothing left unsaid, and there is no dharma that he has understood and yet abandoned; this is called “no knowing-and-yet-abandoning.” Seventh, no diminishment of desire: the Buddha, compassionate toward sentient beings, desires to save them, and his mind knows no satiety; this is called “no diminishment of desire.” Eighth, no diminishment of vigor: the Buddha takes the salvation of all sentient beings as his own task, and so always saves them without rest; this is called “no diminishment of vigor.” Ninth, no diminishment of mindfulness: the Buddha’s dharmas and all the wisdoms of the Buddhas of the three times correspond and are complete without regression; this is called “no diminishment of mindfulness.” Tenth, no diminishment of wisdom: the Buddha possesses all wisdom, measureless and unbounded, beyond exhaustion; hence “no diminishment of wisdom.” Eleventh, no diminishment of liberation: the Buddha is far removed from all attachment and possesses two kinds of liberation — one is the conditioned liberation (the liberation that accords with undefiled wisdom), the other the unconditioned liberation (that in which all defilements are cleansed without remainder); this is called “no diminishment of liberation.” Twelfth, no diminishment of the knowledge and vision of liberation: within all liberations the Buddha’s knowledge and vision are clear and his discernment unobstructed; this is called “no diminishment of the knowledge and vision of liberation.” Thirteenth, all bodily karma follows wisdom: all the Buddha’s bodily actions are led by wisdom, so that none lacks wisdom; this is called “all bodily karma following wisdom.” Fourteenth, all verbal karma follows wisdom: all the Buddha’s spoken words are likewise led by wisdom, so that none lacks wisdom; this is called “all verbal karma following wisdom.” Fifteenth, all mental karma follows wisdom: all the Buddha’s mental reflections are likewise led by wisdom, so that none lacks wisdom; this is called “all mental karma following wisdom.” Sixteenth, unobstructed wisdom knowing the past: the Buddha, with wisdom, illumines all the dharmas of the past and knows them universally without obstruction; this is called “unobstructed wisdom knowing the past.” Seventeenth, unobstructed wisdom knowing the future: the Buddha, with wisdom, illumines all things of the future and knows them universally without obstruction; this is called “unobstructed wisdom knowing the future.” Eighteenth, unobstructed wisdom knowing the present: the Buddha, with wisdom, illumines all things of the present and knows them universally without obstruction; this is called “unobstructed wisdom knowing the present.”

[Dragon King!
