Just as all cities, towns and villages rest upon the great earth and are securely established, and just as all medicinal herbs, plants, trees and thickets alike grow by relying upon the earth, so too are these ten wholesome karma paths. All humans and gods stand firm by depending on them; all the bodhi of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, the practices of the bodhisattvas, and all the Buddha-dharma — together they rely upon this great earth of the ten wholesome karma paths and thereby are accomplished.]

The World-Honored One concluded, saying: Dragon King! Just as all cities, towns and villages rest upon the great earth and are securely established, and just as all medicinal herbs, plants, trees and thickets alike grow by relying upon the great earth, so too is it with these ten wholesome karma paths. All the human vehicle and the divine vehicle stand firm by depending on them; all the śrāvaka vehicle, the pratyekabuddha vehicle, the bodhisattva vehicle, and all the Buddha-dharma together rely upon this great earth of the ten wholesome karma paths and thereby are accomplished.

[When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the Dragon King Sāgara and the great assembly, together with all the gods, humans and asuras of the world, all greatly rejoiced and believed, received and practiced it.]

When the World-Honored One had finished speaking, the Dragon King Sāgara and the assembly present at the Dharma gathering, together with all the gods, humans and asuras of the world, were all filled with the joy of the Dharma and believed, received and practiced it.
The key to gaining the benefit of reciting the sutras and hearing the Dharma lies in these four words: “believing, receiving and practicing.”

[Believing, receiving and practicing] Truly and sincerely believing and receiving the Dharma spoken by the Tathāgata, and earnestly putting into practice the Dharma spoken by the Tathāgata. To hold and practice carries the sense of keeping it deeply in the heart — that is, never forgetting the Buddha’s words in a single thought, and never acting against the Buddha’s words in a single thought.

In reading the sutras and hearing the Dharma, the key is to grasp it for oneself and take it to heart. Take the Buddha’s words as a bright mirror, and reflect upon oneself at all times and in all places; take the Buddha’s words as a beacon, and advance according to the teachings. In one’s cultivation one must firmly grasp these three links — hearing, reflecting and practicing — bringing hearing and reflecting to bear upon practice; only then does one gain true benefit.

[The Three Wisdoms] First, the wisdom of hearing: the wisdom born from seeing and hearing the sutras and teachings. Second, the wisdom of reflection: the wisdom born from pondering the principles. Third, the wisdom of cultivation: the wisdom born from practice. The first two wisdoms are scattered wisdoms, serving as the conditions that give rise to the wisdom of cultivation; the wisdom of cultivation is a wisdom of concentration, which has the function of severing delusion and realizing truth.

blocks.text: Appendix: On Rebuilding the Life-Release Pond at Nanxun Jile Temple

inline.s: Master Yinguang

The matter of abstaining from killing and releasing life is shallow and easy to perceive; the principle of abstaining from killing and releasing life is deep and hard to understand. If one does not understand the principle, though one may carry out the act, the mind can never become sincerely compassionate; the merit and blessings of its field of merit likewise become shallow and slight in keeping with the measure of one’s mind. Should one meet with the obstruction and slander of those who do not understand, one may well be turned about by them, and with that a whole good heart is extinguished. Therefore, without avoiding a surplus of words, I set forth its meaning, so that creatures alike may bathe in compassionate kindness and human relationships may each cultivate their well-being. With the most earnest and profound benevolence we extinguish the retribution of killing for self and other, together reaching the realm of longevity and sharing the joy of a full life. Still further, I pray that this merit be dedicated to the Western Land, so that one may forever emerge from the wheel of transmigration, soaring above the three realms, to be a disciple of Amitābha Buddha and a good companion in the great ocean of beings. May the reader pay heed to this.

Originally, the one-thought mind-nature of the creatures of water and land is, at once, not the least different from that of the Buddhas of the three times. But because the power of karma from past evil deeds has obscured the wondrous brightness, it cannot manifest, and they sink into other classes of beings. Thus their knowledge is mean and inferior: apart from seeking food and escaping death, they know nothing at all. It is like a great precious bronze mirror that for kalpas has been veiled in dust. Not only is it wholly without brightness — even the mirror’s own bronze substance does not appear, and it is just like a useless object. Suddenly it meets a wise person who knows that this is a precious mirror endowed with the boundless light that illumines heaven and earth. He therefore polishes it day after day: at first the mirror’s substance is slightly revealed, next its brightness gradually shines forth, and when the polishing is carried to the utmost, the light that illumines heaven and earth is manifested in its entirety. Only then does the unwise person come to treasure it and regard it as a supreme jewel. One must know that this light the mirror has possessed from the very beginning — it is not obtained from the polishing. Although it is inherently possessed, if there were no condition of polishing, then from kalpa to kalpa there would be no day when it would shine.

The mind-nature of all the beings of the six realms, human and divine, is entirely like this. From beginningless time defilement and karma have obscured it, so that the wondrous brightness inherently present cannot be displayed; deluded and turning against their true nature, they create the karma of birth and death. The Great One Awakened, the World-Honored One, knows that the one-thought mind-nature of all sentient beings is the same as that of the Buddha. For this reason, by various expedient means, he speaks the Dharma in accordance with their capacities, universally causing beings to cultivate the path of precepts, concentration and wisdom, so that, by severing defilement and karma, they may recover what is originally theirs, perfect their merit and wisdom, and realize the Dharma body. He also causes the people of the world to arouse a mind of compassion and abstain from killing and release life. This is because I and all sentient beings are all within the wheel of transmigration. From beginningless time we have been born and reborn one another in turn, and killed one another in turn. They have each in turn been my father, my mother, my elder and younger brothers, my elder and younger sisters, my sons and daughters; and I too have in turn been their father, mother, brothers, sisters, sons and daughters. They indeed, by the power of their evil karma, whether in the human realm or in other classes, have repeatedly suffered my slaughter; and I too, by the power of my evil karma, whether in the human realm or in other classes, have repeatedly suffered their slaughter. Through long kalpas, mutually giving birth and mutually killing, there is no end to it. Ordinary people do not know this; the Tathāgata sees it clearly. Now, having been taught and knowing this for oneself, if one does not reflect on it there is nothing to say, but when one does reflect on it, one is overcome with a shame and compassion beyond bearing!

Now I have been fortunate to inherit the merit and good karma of past lives and am born in the human realm. Surely I ought to dissolve enmity and loosen the knots, abstain from killing and release life, and cause all sentient beings to each gain their proper place. Moreover, for their sake I recite the Buddha and dedicate the merit to the Pure Land, so that they may attain deliverance. Even if, their karma being heavy, they cannot be reborn there immediately, I shall rely upon this compassionate and virtuous merit and earnestly seek, at the end of life, to be reborn in the Western Land. Once reborn there, one at once transcends the ordinary and enters the holy, ends birth and death, forever escapes transmigration, and gradually realizes the Buddha fruit.

Moreover, loving creatures and releasing life — the ancient sages and worthies all practiced this. Thus the Book of Documents has the passage, “Birds, beasts, fish and turtles all are thus,” meaning that birds, beasts, fish and turtles should all be allowed to follow their natural inclinations, free from the suffering of being killed and the terror of being startled; and King Wen’s grace reached even to dry bones — how much the more to creatures possessed of consciousness! As for Jianzi releasing the turtle-dove, Zichan keeping the fish, the Marquis of Sui rescuing the snake, and Yang Bao saving the sparrow — these are indeed the impartial hearts of the sages and worthies who regard all alike, yet they did not yet know that all moving, breathing beings possess the Buddha-nature, that they rise and sink in mutual turn becoming now enemies and now kin, and the principle that in the future they are certain to realize Buddhahood. When the great teaching came east, the causality of the three times and the truth that the mind-natures of sentient beings and of the Buddha are equal and undifferentiated were greatly revealed to the world. Every great sage and worthy has taken abstaining from killing and releasing life as the foundation for turning back the calamity of slaughter to cultivate the fruit of blessing, for stilling the weapons of war and joyfully enjoying a full life.

The ancients said, “If you would know the calamity of weapons in the world, you must hearken to the sound at the butcher’s door in the dead of night.” And again, “If you would have the world free of the calamity of weapons, it is only if sentient beings do not eat flesh.” From this one knows that abstaining from killing and releasing life is the good remedy for saving the world by plucking up its roots. Therefore the Great Master of Tiantai bought more than sixty places along the riverbanks and streams of Linhai, extending over four hundred li, as a life-release pond. He requested that an imperial edict erect a stele forbidding fishing and catching; and those who secretly fished would readily bring misfortune upon themselves. Even down to the Zhenguan era of the Tang it was still so. In the second year of the Qianyuan era of Tang Suzong, an edict was issued to all the prefectures of the empire to each establish a life-release pond, and the emperor commanded Yan Zhenqing to compose the stele inscription and to write it in his own hand. It said, “Our sovereign takes the whole world as a pond, and all within the realm receive blessing; relying upon the sustaining power of the dhāraṇī, he exhausts the sea of affliction and the ford of birth and death. Compared with ancient times, what could ever resemble this?”

Someone says: Widowers, widows, orphans and the childless, the poor and the afflicted, are to be found everywhere; why do you not relieve them, and instead eagerly busy yourself with creatures of another class with whom you have no concern? Are not the urgent and the important thus reversed?

I reply: You do not understand the reason why the Tathāgata teaches people to abstain from killing and release life. Although humans and creatures differ, the Buddha-nature is originally the same. They have fallen into other classes through karmic evil; we have fortunately obtained a human body through karmic good. If we do not extend them compassion but give free rein to eating them, then once our fortune is exhausted and their offenses are discharged, we cannot but be called upon to repay it all and fill their mouth and belly. One must know that the great calamity of weapons is all induced by the karma of killing in past lives. If there were no killing karma, even though one might encounter bandits and thieves, they would arouse good thoughts and would not put one to death. Moreover, in the sudden disasters of plague, flood and fire, those who abstain from killing and release life very rarely meet with them. From this one knows that protecting life is originally protecting oneself. Abstaining from killing can avert being killed by heaven, killed by ghosts and spirits, killed by thieves and robbers, and the future killing of vengeance upon vengeance. As for widowers, widows, orphans and the childless, the poor and the afflicted, one should likewise relieve them according to one’s lot and strength. Could one who abstains from killing and releases life never perform this sort of merit? Yet whereas widowers, widows, orphans and the childless, the poor and the afflicted, are indeed deeply to be pitied, they have not yet reached the point of death. Creatures offered as food, on the other hand, if not promptly ransomed, in a moment find themselves upon the cauldron to fill the belly.
Again he says: The creatures set before us are without end; how many can you possibly release?

I reply: One must understand that the matter of releasing life is in fact the most excellent good heart for arousing people everywhere to protect the lives of beings. We hope that, entering into the spirit of releasing life, they will feel compassion in their hearts and be unable to bear eating them. Since they do not eat them, the catchers will desist. Then all creatures that move in air, on land and in water will freely fly, walk and swim within their own surroundings, so that it becomes a universal release without any actual releasing. Is this not taking the whole world as a pond? Even if not every person can be like this, yet if a single person cannot bear to eat flesh, then measureless lives on land and in water are spared from slaughter — how much the more when there is more than one such person! At the same time, for all present and future companions who abstain from killing and release life, it severs the cause of widowhood, orphanhood, childlessness, poverty and affliction, and forms the condition of long life and freedom from illness, of wealth and honor, peace and happiness, the reunion of father and son, and the sharing of old age by husband and wife. This is precisely to offer relief in advance, so that in life after life and generation after generation they will never suffer the miseries of the widower, the widow, the orphan and the childless, but will long enjoy the happiness of long life, wealth and honor. Is this not a matter of “bringing blessing to the whole realm”? How can one treat it with indifference? Consider it carefully — in abstaining from killing and releasing life, are we eagerly laboring on behalf of people, or eagerly laboring on behalf of creatures, and so reversing the urgent and the important?

Outside the Jile Temple at Nanxun there has long been a life-release pond. Because the embankments were not wholly built, it collapsed. Moreover, for many years it has not been dredged, being filled with silt; and often good-hearted people would release life in the river there. Though they aroused a good intention, the released beings found it hard to gain benefit. Of those released at dawn and re-caught by evening, such were the greater part. If close to a great river, it is right to release them in the river; for a small stream it is by no means appropriate. Master Yuanlin, unable to bear the sight of such dawn-release and dusk-capture, intended to have the pond dredged deep, and to build a wall outside as protection, so that the released would have a place and thieving capture would have no way — his intention, too, was most kind. Before the work had begun, the three Masters Jue of Putuo happened to arrive, and at first meeting their aims were found to accord. He thereupon entrusted the affairs of the monastery to them, while he himself laid down all entanglements and devoted himself solely to Pure Land practice. Master Jue, taking up the former task, wished to bring the matter quickly to completion. But since the project was vast and alone difficult to finish, he proposed to solicit the good and faithful of the whole town to join together in this excellent undertaking, and so asked me to write a preface.

I have often grieved over the cruelty of the calamity of killing in recent times, and though I wished to turn it back I had no strength; because of his request my own heart was stirred. I therefore have briefly set forth the true mind inherently possessed by us and by the creatures, their rising and sinking in accord with karma, and the present and future retributions of killing life and protecting life. I hope that all benefactors will together arouse good thoughts and together donate pure funds, so that this undertaking may speedily succeed, and the creatures may each gain their due place. The merit and benefit are measureless and boundless. Not only will the myriad ills of the present world melt away like ice and the thousand auspicious omens gather like clouds, but in future worlds those who will bear its grace and repay its kindness — who knows how many tens of thousands of millions they will be!

The matter of abstaining from killing and releasing life is shallow and easy to perceive, while the principle of abstaining from killing and releasing life is deep and hard to understand. If one does not understand the principle, then however much one may carry out the act, there is by no means a sincerely compassionate heart; and the blessings of its field of merit likewise become small and shallow in keeping with the narrowness of one’s mind. Should one meet with the obstruction and slander of those who do not understand the principle, it is very likely that one’s original intention will change, and with it the whole good heart will be extinguished. Therefore, here, I do not avoid prolixity, in order to set forth the principle of abstaining from killing and releasing life — so that creatures alike may bathe in compassionate kindness and humans may each cultivate their well-being. With the most earnest and sincere universal love we extinguish the retribution of killing for self and others, together enjoying long life and sharing the joy of full years. And I pray that, with this merit, we dedicate it to rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. Then we shall forever escape transmigration, soaring above the three realms, to be a disciple of Amitābha Buddha and a good companion of the pure great assembly. May the reader peruse it with care.

Originally, the mind-nature of the creatures of water and land is wholly the same as that of the Buddhas of the three times. It is only that, because of evil karma from past lives, the wondrous true mind has been obscured and cannot manifest, so that they have fallen into other classes of beings. Thus their knowledge is mean and inferior: apart from seeking food and escaping death, they know nothing at all. It is like a great precious bronze mirror that for countless kalpas has been covered with dust. Not only is it entirely without brightness — even the very substance of the mirror does not appear, so that it is just like a useless object. Suddenly it meets a wise person who knows it is a precious mirror endowed with the boundless light that illumines heaven and earth. He therefore polishes it day after day: at first the mirror’s substance is slightly exposed, then gradually its light shines forth, and when the polishing is carried to the utmost, the light that illumines heaven and earth is manifested in its fullness. Only then does the unwise person come to know its worth and regard it as a supreme treasure. One must realize that this light is something the precious mirror possessed from the first — it is not obtained through the polishing. Although the mirror inherently possesses it, if there were no condition of polishing, then from kalpa to kalpa there would be no day when it would shine.

The mind-nature of all the beings of the human, divine and six realms is entirely like this. From beginningless kalpas defilement and karma have obscured it, so that the wondrous brightness inherent in them cannot be displayed; deluded and turning away from the true nature, they create the karma of birth and death. The Great Awakened World-Honored One, Śākyamuni Buddha, knows that the mind-nature of all sentient beings is the same as the Buddha’s. For this reason, by many skillful means, he speaks the Dharma according to their capacities, universally causing beings to cultivate the bodhi path of precepts, concentration and wisdom, so that by severing defilement and karma they may recover what is originally theirs, perfect merit and wisdom, and realize the Dharma body. He likewise causes the people of the world to arouse a compassionate heart and abstain from killing and release life. This is because I and all sentient beings are all within the wheel of transmigration. From beginningless kalpas we have been mutually born and mutually killed in turn. They have each in turn been my parents, my brothers and sisters, my sons and daughters; and I too have in turn been their parents, brothers, sisters, sons and daughters. They indeed, through the power of evil karma, whether as humans or as other classes, have suffered my slaughter; and I too, through the power of evil karma, whether as humans or as other classes, have suffered their slaughter. Through long kalpas, mutually begetting and mutually slaying, there is no end. The ordinary person does not know this; the Tathāgata sees it clearly. Now, having received the Buddha’s instruction and knowing it for oneself, if one does not reflect on it then nothing need be said, but when one does reflect on it, how one is overwhelmed with shame and pity!

Now I have been fortunate to inherit the merit, virtue and good karma of past lives and am born in the human realm. Surely I ought to dissolve enmity and untie the knots of resentment, abstain from killing and release life, and cause all living beings to each gain their proper place. And for their sake I recite the Buddha and dedicate the merit to the Pure Land, so that they may attain deliverance. Even if, their karma being heavy, they cannot be reborn immediately, I shall rely upon this compassionate and virtuous merit, and at the end of life shall certainly be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. Once reborn there, one at once transcends the ordinary and enters the holy, ending birth and death and forever escaping transmigration, gradually realizing the Buddha fruit.

Moreover, loving creatures and releasing life — the ancient sages and worthies all practiced it. Thus the Book of Documents has the passage, “Birds, beasts, fish and turtles all are thus,” meaning that birds, beasts, fish and turtles should all be allowed to follow their own natures, free from the pain of being killed and the terror of being startled; and King Wen’s grace extended even to dry bones — how much more to creatures possessed of feeling and consciousness! As for Jianzi releasing the turtle-dove, Zichan raising the fish, the Marquis of Sui aiding the snake, and Yang Bao rescuing the sparrow — these are indeed the impartial, all-for-one hearts of the sages and worthies; yet they did not yet know that all moving, breathing beings are endowed with the Buddha-nature, that they rise and sink in mutual turn becoming now enemies and now kin, and the principle that they will certainly in the future achieve Buddhahood. When the great teaching reached our land, the causality of the three times and the truth that the mind-natures of sentient beings and of the Buddha are equal and undivided were made clear to the world. All the great sages and worthies have taken abstaining from killing and releasing life as the basis for turning back the calamity of slaughter, cultivating the fruit of blessing, stilling the weapons of war, and joyfully fulfilling the years of a natural life.

[Jianzi releasing the turtle-dove] This is the story from the Warring States period of the feudal lord Zhao Jianzi releasing turtle-doves. On New Year’s Day (the first day of the first month) a man of Handan presented turtle-doves to Zhao Jianzi. Zhao Jianzi was greatly delighted and rewarded him generously. A guest asked him why he was so happy. Zhao Jianzi replied: “I am about to release them, so as to show my kindness and favor.” The guest said: “Once everyone knows you are releasing them, they will all cater to your tastes and vie with one another to catch them for you to set free. With this catching and releasing, the number that are hurt and die will be many. If you truly wish not to harm them, the best course is to forbid the catching. If you catch them and then release them, your kindness cannot outweigh your fault.” Zhao Jianzi gladly adopted this advice and issued an order strictly forbidding the capture. [Zichan raising the fish] Someone presented fish to Zichan (a disciple of Confucius); unable to bear seeing them killed, he put them all into the pond. [The Marquis of Sui aiding the snake] The Marquis of Sui, on his way to the state of Qi, saw upon the road a snake trapped in a sandy place with its head bleeding. He lifted it with his staff and placed it in the water. On his return he again passed that place, and the snake came bearing a precious pearl in its mouth to present to him. [Yang Bao rescuing the sparrow] When Yang Bao was young, he saw a yellow sparrow struck and wounded by an owl and fallen to the ground, encircled by a swarm of ants. He picked up the yellow bird, carried it home, placed it in a box, and fed it with yellow blossoms. When the wound healed, he let it fly away. That night he dreamed of a youth in yellow robes who bowed in thanks and presented him with four jade rings, saying: “I am the messenger of the Queen Mother of the West. I owe my life to your rescue. Your descendants will all be of noble integrity, of wealth and honor, ranked among the Three Dukes, even as these four rings.” Afterwards, for four generations, the line of Yang Bao was distinguished and honored.

The ancients said, “If you would know the calamity of weapons in the world, you must hearken to the sound at the butcher’s door in the dead of night.” And again, “If you would have the world without the calamity of weapons, it is only if sentient beings do not eat flesh.” From this one knows that abstaining from killing and releasing life is the good means that saves the world by drawing out its very root. Therefore the Great Master of Tiantai bought over sixty places along the riverbanks of Linhai, stretching more than four hundred li, as a life-release pond. He also requested the court to erect a stele forbidding fishing and catching, and those who secretly fished were strictly punished. Even down to the Zhenguan era of the Tang it was still so. In the second year of the Qianyuan era of Tang Suzong, an edict was issued to the empire commanding each prefecture to establish a life-release pond; the emperor, by imperial decree, commanded Yan Zhenqing (the great calligrapher, who rose to Minister of Personnel and Grand Preceptor to the Crown Prince, enfeoffed as Duke of Lu) to compose the inscription and to have it engraved upon stone. The inscription read: “Our wise sovereign takes the whole world as a pond, and all within the realm receive blessing; relying upon the sustaining power of the sacred mantra, he exhausts the ford of birth and death in the sea of affliction. When one examines all the ages past, how could there ever have been such a work?”

In the first year of the Tianxi era of Song Zhenzong, an edict was issued to the empire establishing life-release ponds; and West Lake at Hangzhou was likewise a life-release pond of the Song dynasty. In the Ming, Great Master Lianchi established life-release ponds at the two places of Shangfang and Changshou. His Essay on Abstaining from Killing and Releasing Life has been circulated throughout the world. In the more than three hundred years down to the present, of the monks and laymen who have admired his lofty conduct and compassionately aided creatures — how could they be counted?

Someone asks: Widowers, widows, orphans and the childless, the poor and the afflicted, are everywhere; why do you not relieve them, and instead rush about busily rescuing creatures of another class with whom we have no concern? Are not the urgent and the important thus reversed?

I reply: You do not know the reason why the Tathāgata teaches people to abstain from killing and release life. Although humans and creatures differ, the Buddha-nature is the same. It is because of evil karma that they have fallen into other classes; it is because of good karma that we have fortunately obtained a human body. If we do not pity them but give free rein to eating them, then once our fortune is spent and their offenses discharged, we cannot escape being called to repay it all, and be eaten by them. One must know that the great calamity of weapons is all induced by the karma of killing in past lives. If there were no killing karma, even if one met with bandits and thieves, they would arouse good thoughts and would not harm one. Moreover, in the sudden disasters of plague, flood and fire, those who abstain from killing and release life very rarely encounter them. From this one knows that protecting life is originally protecting oneself. Abstaining from killing can avoid being killed by heaven, killed by ghosts and spirits, killed by robbers and thieves, and the future killing of revenge upon revenge. As for widowers, widows, orphans and the childless, the poor and the afflicted, one ought also, according to one’s lot and strength, to extend them relief. Could one who abstains from killing and releases life never perform this sort of merit? Yet although widowers, widows, orphans and the childless, the poor and the afflicted, are deeply to be pitied, they have not yet reached the point of death. The creatures set before us as food, on the other hand, if not ransomed at once, are immediately boiled and devoured to fill the belly.
Again he asks: The creatures offered as food are beyond counting; how many can you release?

I reply: One must realize that the matter of releasing life is in truth the most excellent good intention for arousing people everywhere to protect the lives of creatures. We hope that, embodying the meaning of releasing life, they will feel pity in their hearts and be unable to bear eating them. Since they do not eat them, there will be none to catch them. Then all creatures in air, on land and in water will freely fly, run and swim within their own dwelling-places, becoming a universal release even though no release is performed. Is this not to take the whole world as a pond? Even if not every person can be like this, yet if one person cannot bear to eat flesh, then measureless lives on land and in water are spared from slaughter — how much the more when there are far more than one! Moreover, this severs, for all present and future companions who abstain from killing and release life, the cause of widowhood, orphanhood, childlessness, poverty and affliction, and forms the condition of long life, freedom from illness, wealth, honor, peace and happiness, the reunion of father and son, and husband and wife growing old together. It is precisely to offer relief in advance, so that in life after life they will never again suffer the miseries of the widower, the widow, the orphan and the childless, but will long enjoy the happiness of longevity, wealth and honor. Is this not a matter of “bringing blessing to every place”? How can one regard it with indifference? Consider it yourself — in abstaining from killing and releasing life, is one eagerly laboring for people, or eagerly laboring for creatures, and so reversing the urgent and the important?

Outside the Jile Temple at Nanxun there has long been a life-release pond. Because the embankments were not wholly completed, it gave way. Moreover, for many years it has not been dredged, so that it is filled with silt; and often good-hearted people would release life in this river. Though they aroused a good intention, the released beings found it hard to gain benefit. Of those released at dawn and caught again by evening, such are the majority. If close to a great river, then it is right to release them in the river; for a small stream it is by no means suitable. Master Yuanlin, unable to bear the sight of dawn-release and dusk-capture, intended to have this pond dredged deep, and to build a wall outside for protection, so that there would be a place for releasing life and no way for thieves to catch them — his intention, too, was most kind. Before the work had begun, the three Masters Jue of Putuo happened to arrive, and at the very first meeting their aims were found to accord. Master Yuanlin then entrusted to them the affairs of the monastery, while he himself put down all entanglements and devoted himself solely to the Pure Land practice. Master Jue, taking up the former undertaking, wished to bring the matter speedily to completion. But since the project was vast and his strength alone could not accomplish it, he proposed to solicit the good and faithful of the whole town to join together in this excellent work, and so asked me to write a preface.

I have often sorrowed over the cruelty of the calamity of killing in recent times, and though I wished to turn it back I had no power; because of his request my own heart was deeply moved. I therefore have briefly here set forth the true mind inherently possessed by humans and by creatures, their rising and sinking in accord with karma, and the present and future retributions of killing and of protecting life. I hope that all ladles and benefactors will together arouse good thoughts and together give pure funds, so that this undertaking may speedily be accomplished, and the creatures may each gain their due place. The merit and benefit is measureless and boundless. Not only will the myriad calamities of the present world melt away like ice and the thousand auspicious signs gather like clouds — but in future worlds, those who will receive its grace and repay its kindness, how many tens of thousands of millions, who can say!
